extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, logicians, and scholars concerned with defining terms and scientific terminology
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for fixing precise connotations/definitions of terms used in science and philosophy, balancing current usage, historical meaning, and usefulness for expressing propositions and discovering truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix connotation in agreement with received use
rubrics_metrics.description: The fixed and precise connotation which a term receives should not be in deviation from, but in agreement (as far as it goes) with, the vague and fluctuating connotation which the term already had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, define a name so it continues to denote the same objects and preserves received assertions; avoid redefining so as to render established true propositions inadmissible. Only define a term differently when there is strong reason and awareness of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define names by comparing attributes of the denoted objects
rubrics_metrics.description: To fix the connotation of a concrete name ... is to define the name. This supposes a comparison of the things, feature by feature and property by property, to ascertain what attributes they agree in; and not unfrequently an operation strictly inductive, for the purpose of ascertaining some unobvious agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine common attributes by systematic comparison and, where needed, induction to discover non-obvious shared properties before selecting which to include in a definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer well-known properties but select those that best mark the class
rubrics_metrics.description: Our choice is first limited by the preference to be given to properties which are well known, and familiarly predicated of the class; but even these are often too numerous ... the properties most generally known may not be those which serve best to mark out the class from all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor properties familiar to usage, but prioritize properties that distinguish the class most effectively from others; balance recognizability with discriminatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select properties on which many others depend (causal or inferential marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: We should therefore select from among the common properties ... those on which it has been ascertained by experience, or proved by deduction, that many others depend; or at least which are sure marks of them, and from whence, therefore, many others will follow by inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many common properties exist, choose defining marks that are causally or logically upstream — features that imply or generate other properties — so the definition yields useful inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be tied to propositions and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: To unfold our conceptions by means of definitions has never been serviceable to science, except when it has been associated with an immediate use of the definitions ... that which alone makes it worth while to explain it in any mode, is the opportunity of using it in the expression of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what proposition or principle the definition serves to express; a definition gains scientific value only when it is used to state or test a principle or truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are part of discovery and require sagacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of definition is part of the business of discovery.... To define, so that our definition shall have any scientific value, requires no small portion of that sagacity by which truth is detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that choosing a fruitful definition often reflects an advance in knowledge; good definitions may follow or accompany discoveries and require insight into the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow definitions to evolve with advancing science
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to frame a perfect set of definitions on any subject, until the theory of the subject is perfect; and as science makes progress, its definitions are also progressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to revising definitions as theory develops; treat definitions as provisional tools that should track improved understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: When precise connotation would drop important senses, prefer restriction over extension
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better, in such a case, to give a fixed connotation to the term by restricting, than by extending its use; rather excluding from the epithet ... some things to which it is commonly considered applicable, than leaving out of its connotation any of the qualities by which ... the mind may have been habitually guided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fixing a term's meaning forces a choice, prefer narrowing the denotation to preserve salient qualities rather than enlarging it so as to include cases that would erase important senses (example: 'beautiful').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discard portions of traditional connotation without deep knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: In attempting to rectify the use of a vague term by giving it a fixed connotation, we must take care not to discard (unless advisedly, and on the ground of a deeper knowledge of the subject) any portion of the connotation which the word, in however indistinct a manner, previously carried with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve aspects of meaning that embody historical experience; anyone proposing to alter meanings should be well acquainted with the word's history and the opinions it expressed, and ensure no historically held true propositions become falsely excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use predicates and propositions to keep word-meanings alive
rubrics_metrics.description: Words naturally retain much more of their meaning to persons of active imagination ... To minds of a different description, the only antidote to this corruption of language is predication. The habit of predicating of the name, all the various properties which it originally connoted, keeps up the association between the name and those properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively predicate and teach the full cluster of properties associated with a term so that habitual usage does not erode its richer meanings; maintain propositions that preserve the intended sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary or insulated definitions; definitions should reflect the proposition intended
rubrics_metrics.description: These controversies have never been questions of insulated and arbitrary definitions ... In all cases there is a tacit assumption of some proposition which is to be expressed by means of the definition, and which gives it its importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invent definitions in isolation; definitions should be chosen to express the propositions or principles they are meant to serve, otherwise they lack scientific value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of transitive (derivative) applications and blended meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: The applications which a word acquires by this gradual extension of it from one set of objects to another ... Stewart calls its transitive applications ... Where the association is so natural and habitual as to become virtually indissoluble, the transitive meanings will coalesce in one complex conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether multiple senses of a term arose by benign transitions of association; recognize when meanings have coalesced into a complex conception and avoid forcing a single artificial genus onto genuinely distinct senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the history of a word as a guide to current employment
rubrics_metrics.description: The history of a word, by showing the causes which determine its use, is in these cases a better guide to its employment than any definition; for definitions can only show its meaning at the particular time, or at most the series of its successive meanings, but its history may show the law by which the succession was produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When usage is subtle or dictionaries are blunt, study the historical progression and associative causes of a word's meanings to guide correct present-day application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize casual associations can become fixed connotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides common properties ... any other circumstance may casually be found along with it, so frequently as to become associated with it ... The circumstance originally casual, thus becomes regularly a part of the connotation of the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for non-essential but habitual associations (colors, contexts, emotions) that may have become entrenched in meaning; these can meaningfully affect current usage and should inform definition choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries give a blunt, broad meaning; nuance requires usage-history
rubrics_metrics.description: The dictionary meaning is marked out in a broad, blunt way, and probably includes all that was originally necessary for the correct employment of the term; but in process of time so many collateral associations adhere to words, that whoever should attempt to use them with no other guide than the dictionary, would confound a thousand nice distinctions and subtle shades of meaning which dictionaries take no account of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on dictionary definitions for precise scientific or philosophical usage; seek contextual and historical nuance to capture subtle distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of logicians fixing meanings at a low-significance moment
rubrics_metrics.description: It sometimes happens ... persons arise whose leading and favorite idea is the importance of clear conceptions and precise thought ... they define the name without reference to [the old connotation] ... they fasten down the name to what it connotes in common use at the time when it conveys the smallest quantity of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of reforms that crystallize a word's meaning at the stage when it has least of its historical sense preserved; such fixation can prematurely discard valuable past meanings and retard later recovery.
